questions.question: An EIGRP topology table shows two paths to a remote prefix: the SUCCESSOR (lowest FD via current next-hop) and an alternative path that satisfies the FEASIBILITY CONDITION (its reported distance < successor's FD). When the successor link drops, EIGRP installs the feasible successor IMMEDIATELY — no recomputation. Which EIGRP algorithm provides this loop-free convergence?
options: DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm)
Load-balancing algorithm — different concept (variance + equal/unequal cost)
OSPF optimisation — different protocol entirely (SPF / Dijkstra)
Spanning Tree variant — L2 loop prevention, not L3 routing
questions.explanation: DUAL runs in EIGRP to select loop-free routes. It maintains the Successor (best path) and Feasible Successors (backup paths meeting FC). Avoids Dijkstra's CPU-intensive SPF calculation while guaranteeing loop-free convergence.

questions.question: An OSPF design uses three area variants at the edge to reduce LSDB size. Variant A blocks External LSAs (Type 5) — receives a default route instead. Variant B blocks Type 5 AND Type 3/4 — only a default. Variant C is like A but ALLOWS local redistribution from external protocols as Type 7. Which mapping is correct?
options: Stub blocks all routing — false; stub allows intra-area routing
NSSA is only for BGP — false; NSSA is an OSPF area type
All three are identical — false
Stub: blocks Type 5 LSAs
questions.explanation: Stub area: no Type 5 (external) LSAs, uses default route. Totally stubby (Cisco): no Type 3 or Type 5 LSAs. NSSA: blocks Type 5 but allows redistribution via Type 7 (converted to Type 5 by ABR). Reduces LSDB size. Totally stubby: also blocks inter-area LSAs (Type 3). NSSA: like stub but allows limited external route import via Type 7 LSAs — for areas with non-OSPF routing

questions.question: Inside an Autonomous System with 50 iBGP speakers, a naive design requires (50 × 49 / 2) = 1225 iBGP peerings (full mesh) because iBGP has split-horizon: routes received from one iBGP peer are NOT re-advertised to other iBGP peers. What Cisco feature allows a ROUTE REFLECTOR (RR) to relay iBGP routes to its CLIENTS, eliminating the full-mesh requirement?
options: BGP Route Reflection — a Route Reflector reflects iBGP routes among its clients, eliminating the full-mesh requirement by allowing clients to learn routes through the RR
BGP confederation — subdivides the AS into sub-ASes that use eBGP-like sessions internally, reducing iBGP full-mesh sessions but without a dedicated RR-clients relationship
BGP authentication — adds MD5 or TCP-AO to iBGP sessions for security; does not reduce the number of sessions or eliminate the full-mesh requirement
BGP route dampening — suppresses flapping routes to improve stability; does not affect the iBGP full-mesh topology or the number of iBGP sessions required
questions.explanation: iBGP requires full mesh (every router peers with every other). With N routers: N(N-1)/2 sessions. Route Reflectors break this: clients peer only with RR; RR re-advertises routes. Confederations are the alternative solution. a Route Reflector (RR) re-advertises iBGP routes to its clients, eliminating the need for all routers to peer with each other (O(n²) problem)

questions.question: An MPLS-enabled core has hundreds of LSRs forwarding packets by label-swapping. Each LSR must learn which label its UPSTREAM neighbour uses for a given FEC. Cisco IOS-XR uses a control protocol that runs on TCP 646 to advertise label-to-FEC bindings between LSRs. Which protocol is this?
options: LDP (Label Distribution Protocol)
An IGP — distributes routes, not MPLS labels
An encryption protocol — orthogonal
A multicast routing protocol — different surface
questions.explanation: LDP (or TDP, RSVP-TE for traffic engineering) establishes label-to-FEC (Forwarding Equivalency Class) bindings between Label Switching Routers. Each LSR maintains a Label Information Base (LIB) and forwards packets using label lookup.

questions.question: Cisco IOS marks packets with a QoS field in the IP header. The MODERN marker uses 6 BITS of the IP TOS / Traffic Class byte (giving 64 possible values, e.g., EF, AF41, CS6, DSCP 46). The LEGACY marker used 3 bits (8 values, IP Precedence). The modern marker is a superset that includes the legacy via Class Selector codepoints. Which statement is correct?
options: DSCP and IP Precedence use DIFFERENT header fields — false; both use the same TOS / Traffic Class byte
DSCP only marks voice — false; DSCP marks all classes (voice, video, bulk, etc.)
DSCP (RFC 2474) = 6 bits, 64 values
IP Precedence is modern, DSCP is legacy — reversed
questions.explanation: DSCP uses 6 bits of the original ToS byte (IP header), allowing 64 PHB (Per-Hop Behavior) values. Expedited Forwarding (EF/46): low latency for voice. Assured Forwarding (AF): guaranteed minimum bandwidth. CS (Class Selector): backward compat with IP Precedence.

questions.question: A multi-site enterprise wants to: (a) decouple WAN policy from hardware vendor, (b) use multiple transports (MPLS + broadband + LTE) actively, (c) centralise policy (URL filtering, QoS, app routing) via a controller, (d) push intent-based config to branch CPEs. Which technology?
options: Software-Defined WAN (SD-WAN)
Software-Defined Data Centre — DC concept, not WAN
Software-Defined Storage — storage abstraction, not WAN
Wireless LAN solution — different domain
questions.explanation: SD-WAN (Cisco Viptela/SDWAN, VMware VeloCloud) centralizes WAN control, enables application-aware routing, automatic failover between WAN links, and reduces costs by using broadband/LTE alongside MPLS.

questions.question: Two tenants share one physical router but must have ISOLATED routing tables — including OVERLAPPING IP space (e.g., both use 10.0.0.0/8). The router provides per-tenant RIB / FIB / interface assignments / routing-protocol instances inside ONE chassis. Which Cisco feature?
options: VLAN — L2 isolation, not L3 routing tables
VRF (Virtual Routing and Forwarding)
STP variant — L2 loop prevention, different concept
Firewall feature — different surface
questions.explanation: VRF creates virtual routers within a physical router, each with its own routing table, forwarding table, and interfaces. Used in MPLS L3 VPNs (VRF-Lite without MPLS), multi-tenant environments, and network segmentation.

questions.question: Routing protocols' Hello timers (OSPF 10s, EIGRP 5s, BGP 60s) are too slow for sub-second link-failure detection. A LIGHTWEIGHT protocol sits BELOW the routing protocols, sends very-frequent (e.g., 50 ms) Hello packets between two endpoints, and notifies the routing protocols on failure. Which protocol?
options: An STP variant — different surface (L2)
Another routing protocol — slower than the documented sub-second target
BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection)
A DHCP variant — different protocol family
questions.explanation: BFD detects failures in milliseconds vs OSPF/EIGRP hello/dead timers (seconds). BFD sessions run independently, notifying routing protocols when failure detected. Supported by OSPF, EIGRP, BGP, IS-IS, and static routes.

questions.question: A network team replaces manual SSH-and-paste with PROGRAMMATIC device configuration. They want IETF-standard protocols: (a) XML/SSH-based for stateful candidate config + commit, (b) REST/HTTP+JSON-based for resource-oriented operations. Both use YANG models. Which two protocols?
options: SSH alternatives — too vague
NETCONF (RFC 6241, XML/SSH, candidate-commit) + RESTCONF (RFC 8040,
A new routing protocol — wrong category
SNMP replacements only — narrower than the question; NETCONF/RESTCONF are configuration-management, not just monitoring
questions.explanation: NETCONF uses XML over SSH for transactional configuration management (commit/rollback). RESTCONF uses REST/HTTP with JSON or XML for simpler programmatic access. Both use YANG data models. Foundation of modern network automation.

questions.question: Cisco's central controller for Intent-Based Networking provides: (a) DESIGN (templates, IP pools, AAA), (b) PROVISIONING (push config to onboarded devices), (c) ASSURANCE (health analytics with ML), (d) POLICY (group-based segmentation, SGT-based access). Which product?
options: Cisco DNA Center (now Catalyst Center)
A security scanner — wrong category
A cloud management portal — different surface (Meraki Dashboard or Intersight)
A standalone routing platform — too narrow
questions.explanation: Cisco DNA Center uses intent (business requirements) to automatically configure network devices consistently. Provides: network design templates, zero-touch provisioning, AI-driven assurance, policy enforcement via SD-Access.

questions.question: An OSPF router needs to inject EIGRP-learned routes into OSPF (cross-protocol redistribution). Two pitfalls must be considered: (a) external routes get OSPF default metric of 20 if no `metric` is set, (b) administrative-distance comparison with the receiving protocol could cause routing loops. What is OSPF route redistribution?
options: OSPF area merging — combines two OSPF areas into one for simplified routing, but does not inject external EIGRP routes into OSPF
BGP route injection — uses BGP to inject external routes into the WAN routing domain rather than redistributing between IGPs
Route redistribution — importing routes from one routing protocol (EIGRP) and re-advertising them into another (OSPF) using `redistribute eigrp <asn>` in OSPF config
VLAN route sharing — extends Layer-2 VLANs across routers for shared route visibility, unrelated to OSPF/EIGRP cross-protocol redistribution
questions.explanation: Redistribution imports routes between protocols (EIGRP↔OSPF, Static↔OSPF). Issues: suboptimal routing, routing loops (two-way redistribution). Mitigations: route tags (mark redistributed routes to prevent re-redistribution), distribute-lists, prefix-lists.

questions.question: Two routers need to encapsulate ANY Layer-3 protocol (IPv4, IPv6, IPX) inside an IP packet to traverse an intermediate network. The encapsulation adds a 4-byte protocol-id header and an outer IP header. The result LOOKS like an IP packet to the intermediate network but transparently carries the inner payload. Which tunnel?
options: Fibre Channel — storage protocol, not L3 tunnel
An IPsec security protocol — different concern (security, not encapsulation per-se)
GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation)
VLAN extension (VXLAN) — different overlay (L2 over L3)
questions.explanation: GRE (Protocol 47) wraps packets in an IP + GRE header, allowing non-IP protocols or multicast over IP networks. GRE itself provides no encryption — combine with IPSec for secure tunnels. Used in DMVPN and SD-WAN. encapsulates virtually any Layer 3 protocol inside IP packets, creating a virtual point-to-point tunnel between endpoints across IP networks

questions.question: A hub-and-spoke WAN with 500 branch offices needs spoke-to-spoke dynamic tunnels (without the hub in the data path) WITHOUT pre-configuring every spoke pair. The Cisco solution combines GRE multipoint (mGRE), NHRP for next-hop resolution, and IPsec for encryption. What is this technology?
options: An SD-WAN product — separate product family (Viptela / Catalyst SD-WAN)
DMVPN
A routing protocol — wrong category
A static VPN — DMVPN is dynamic, not static
questions.explanation: DMVPN phases: Phase 1 (hub-and-spoke, all traffic through hub), Phase 2 (spoke-to-spoke direct tunnels, no summarization), Phase 3 (spoke-to-spoke with summarization via NHRP redirect). Reduces hub load.

questions.question: An ISP backbone runs a link-state IGP that is similar to OSPF but: (a) runs directly over L2 (CLNS) instead of IP, (b) uses two-level hierarchical area design (L1 / L2), (c) is the IGP of choice for many large service-provider networks. Which protocol?
options: IS-IS as distance-vector — false; IS-IS is link-state
IS-IS always faster — context-dependent, not a definition
IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System)
IS-IS is obsolete — false; widely used in SP networks
questions.explanation: IS-IS (ISO 10589) is a link-state protocol using Dijkstra like OSPF. Runs at Layer 2 (IP-independent), making it resilient to IP issues. Uses levels instead of areas. Widely used by large ISP backbones (commonly more than OSPF for ISPs).

questions.question: An ISP wants to route traffic from a VIP customer (source 192.0.2.0/24) via a premium upstream, while other traffic uses the cheaper default path. Standard routing only inspects DESTINATION; the team needs to route based on SOURCE IP. Which Cisco feature overrides the routing table for matching traffic?
options: Path balancing routing — vague, not a real Cisco term
A BGP policy attribute — applies to BGP route exchange, not packet-level forwarding override
Policy-Based Routing (PBR)
A routing protocol — PBR is a forwarding-policy mechanism, not a protocol
questions.explanation: PBR uses route-maps applied to interfaces to forward packets based on ACL matches (source, destination, protocol) to specific next-hops. Use cases: route VoIP to MPLS, route HTTP via broadband, load balancing by source.

questions.question: Cisco's campus network architecture uses: VXLAN overlay fabric, LISP for the overlay control plane, ISE for identity-based policy (SGT tags), and DNA Center for orchestration. Endpoints get a scalable group tag (SGT) and policy is enforced uniformly. What is this called?
options: Cisco SD-Access
A routing protocol — wrong category
Cloud-only solution — false; SD-Access is on-prem campus
A WAN solution — that would be Cisco SD-WAN, separate product
questions.explanation: SD-Access: Underlay (routed access), Overlay (VXLAN/LISP), Policy (ISE+SGT/SGACLs), Management (DNA Center). Virtual Networks (VNs) provide macro-segmentation; Scalable Group Tags (SGTs) provide micro-segmentation.

questions.question: A data centre needs LAYER-2 reachability between racks but the L2 fabric must scale beyond the 4094-VLAN cap and be routed over L3 underlay. Encapsulating an L2 frame in UDP / IP gives an L2 overlay across L3 infrastructure with a 24-bit VNI (16M segments). Which technology?
options: STP replacement — different scope
A new VLAN standard — VXLAN is an overlay, not a VLAN-tag scheme
A multicast protocol — different scope (though BUM traffic uses multicast)
VXLAN
questions.explanation: VXLAN (RFC 7348) uses UDP port 4789 to tunnel Layer 2 frames over IP networks. Solves: 4094 VLAN limit (uses 24-bit VNID = 16M segments), enables Layer 2 adjacency across routed fabrics. Core of modern data center and SD-Access overlays.

questions.question: A multicast deployment uses an explicit-join model: receivers register with a designated Rendezvous Point (RP) by sending PIM Joins toward it; sources register with the RP and traffic is forwarded down the shared tree (or via SPT switchover). The protocol is independent of the unicast routing protocol — relies on whatever IGP is present. Which mode?
options: PIM Sparse Mode
QoS mechanism — wrong concept
PIM Dense Mode — flood-and-prune (the OPPOSITE of explicit-join sparse)
Unicast routing protocol — multicast PIM is for multicast, not unicast
questions.explanation: PIM-SM (RFC 7761) builds shared trees via RP and source trees (SPT). Receivers join via IGMP; PIM Join messages travel toward RP/source. Cisco uses Auto-RP or PIM BSR for RP discovery. SSM (Source Specific Multicast) avoids RP entirely. assumes receivers are sparse. Uses a Rendezvous Point (RP) for initial source/receiver discovery; direct source trees built after RPT path established

questions.question: Cisco ships THREE distinct OS lineages. (A) Modular IOS for enterprise routers and switches (ASR, ISR, Cat9k). (B) Carrier-grade high-availability OS for service-provider edge (ASR9k / NCS). (C) Linux-based DC OS for Nexus switches with VDCs and per-process restart. Which mapping is correct?
options: IOS-XE = enterprise modular IOS (ASR/ISR)
Three names for the same software — false
Different protocols — false; all three are device OSes
Legacy versions — false; all three are current
questions.explanation: IOS-XE: modular architecture (SPA/SIP separation), enterprise-grade. IOS-XR: microkernel, in-service software upgrade (ISSU), massive scale, 32-bit process separation. NX-OS: Linux-based, programmable, feature-rich for data center.

questions.question: A data centre uses an APIC controller to push 'application profiles' that describe ENDPOINT GROUPS (EPGs) and CONTRACTS between them. The fabric (spine-leaf) enforces policy regardless of underlying VLAN/IP. Which Cisco product?
options: Cisco SD-WAN — Cisco's WAN fabric with vManage/vSmart/vBond controllers; uses application-aware routing but not APIC or application profile constructs
Cisco ACI (Application Centric Infrastructure) — uses an APIC controller and application profiles (EPGs, contracts, bridge domains) to define network policy
Cisco DNA Center — Cisco's campus network controller for SD-Access; manages VN/SGT segmentation and application policies but uses a different controller architecture than APIC
Cisco IOS-XE standalone routing — a traditional router platform without a centralised application-profile-driven policy model or APIC controller
questions.explanation: ACI: APIC cluster (3 controllers), Leaf-Spine topology with VXLAN/EVPN overlay. Key concepts: Tenant, VRF, Bridge Domain (BD), Endpoint Group (EPG), Contract (policy). Policy defined in APIC, pushed to spine/leaf hardware.

questions.question: A data-centre fabric needs both L2 (host-mobility, MAC learning across racks) AND L3 (subnet routing) services WITHOUT flood-and-learn. The IETF standard uses MP-BGP as the CONTROL PLANE to advertise MAC + IP + EVI bindings; VXLAN or MPLS carries the data plane. Which standard?
options: An IGP — control plane, but EVPN is a BGP family, not an IGP
Legacy L2VPN — older, no MAC mobility / multi-tenant scale of EVPN
Cisco-proprietary VLAN extension — false; EVPN is an open IETF standard
EVPN (RFC 7432)
questions.explanation: EVPN uses MP-BGP route types (Type 2: MAC/IP, Type 3: Inclusive Multicast, Type 5: IP prefix) as control plane for VXLAN. Replaces flood-and-learn with BGP-based MAC distribution, enabling scalable data center overlays.

questions.question: A network automation team defines DATA MODELS describing the structure of network device configuration in a vendor-neutral way. Models are written in a domain-specific language, used by NETCONF and RESTCONF as the payload schema. What is this language?
options: A scripting tool — wrong category; YANG is a modeling language
A general-purpose programming language — wrong category
A routing protocol — wrong category
YANG (RFC 6020)
questions.explanation: YANG models define the schema for network data — what configuration parameters exist, their types, constraints, and relationships. Vendors publish YANG models for their devices. Tools: pyang (validation), netconf-console, nornir, pyATS. a data modeling language (RFC 7950) that defines the structure of network device configuration and operational state data consumed by NETCONF and RESTCONF

questions.question: An automation team picks an AGENTLESS configuration-management tool. It connects to devices over SSH or NETCONF, executes from declarative YAML playbooks, and ships with hundreds of network modules (`cisco.ios.*`, `cisco.nxos.*`, `arista.eos.*`). Which tool?
options: A routing protocol — wrong category
Ansible
Cisco-specific — false; Ansible is multi-vendor
A Python library — Ansible itself is the tool; it's BUILT in Python but is a tool, not a library
questions.explanation: Ansible uses playbooks (YAML) with network modules (ios_config, nxos_vlan, etc.) to automate device configuration. Agentless (connects via SSH/NETCONF). Idempotent. Popular modules: ios_command, eos_config, junos_config.

questions.question: An engineer building custom network-automation scripts picks a language that has rich libraries for: SSH (Netmiko), multi-vendor NAPALM, JSON/YAML/XML parsing, REST clients (requests), and YANG modelling (pyangbind). The language dominates network automation. Which language?
options: A Cisco product — wrong category
Not relevant — false; the language IS extremely relevant
Python
Only for web development — false; Python is general-purpose
questions.explanation: Python + Netmiko: SSH connections to devices. NAPALM: vendor-neutral API for config/state. Nornir: parallel automation framework. pyATS/Genie: Cisco testing framework. Requests: REST API calls to controllers, cloud APIs.

questions.question: A trunk port connects to a VMware ESXi host's virtual switch (not a real STP-aware switch). With normal STP timing the port spends 30+ seconds listening/learning at link-up, blocking VM traffic. Which Cisco feature allows the trunk port to TRANSITION TO FORWARDING IMMEDIATELY on link-up, and is appropriate when the downstream end is NOT a switch?
options: PortFast trunk mode
PortFast access-only — wrong; the question is about a trunk port
PortFast without BPDU Guard — bad practice; PortFast should pair with BPDU Guard
PortFast on all ports — over-broad and dangerous
questions.explanation: Standard PortFast is for access ports. PortFast trunk is for trunk ports connecting to servers/hypervisors that need rapid forwarding without STP delay but aren't switches. Must still avoid connecting to other switches with this setting.

questions.question: Cisco DNA Center has a module that ingests telemetry from every onboarded device, applies ML / AI to correlate symptoms across devices, surfaces root-cause analysis ('Wi-Fi 5 GHz radio underperforming in building 3'), and recommends remediation steps. What is this module?
options: A security scanner — different surface (DNA Center has Security Adviser but that's compliance)
Cisco DNA Assurance
A config-backup tool — operational utility, not the assurance analytics product
A routing protocol — wrong category
questions.explanation: DNA Assurance provides 360° network visibility with AI-driven insights, AI-driven issue detection, client health scores, application performance monitoring, and natural language search for troubleshooting.

questions.question: An IS-IS hierarchical design uses two levels. ONE level handles intra-area routing (within a single area, analogous to OSPF non-backbone). The OTHER level handles inter-area routing across the backbone (analogous to OSPF Area 0). Routers can be L1, L2, or L1/L2. Which mapping?
options: Deprecated levels — false; both are current
Different protocol versions — false; just different routing scope
Priority levels — false; not priority
Level 1 = intra-area (OSPF non-backbone analog)
questions.explanation: IS-IS levels: L1 = intra-area (knows only own area topology). L2 = inter-area backbone (knows all area prefixes). L1/L2 = both (like OSPF ABR). All L2 routers form a contiguous backbone. No concept of a 'Area 0' like OSPF.

questions.question: Cisco SD-Access uses a control-plane protocol that separates an endpoint's IDENTITY (Endpoint Identifier, EID) from its LOCATION (Routing Locator, RLOC). When an EID moves to a new RLOC (host mobility), the control plane updates the mapping without changing the IP address. Which protocol?
options: A security protocol — wrong category
An encryption protocol — wrong category
A routing protocol — partial truth (LISP IS a routing protocol) but the BEST answer is the identity-location separation property
LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol)
questions.explanation: LISP maps EIDs to RLOCs via a Map-Server/Map-Resolver. When a host moves, only the LISP map changes, not the routing table. In SD-Access, LISP distributes host-to-switch-location mappings across the fabric. IP/MAC) from its location (RLOC — routing locator) — enables mobility without changing routing tables. Used as overlay control plane in Cisco SD-Access

questions.question: An ISP wants to route GOLD-tier customer traffic along a specific path satisfying bandwidth + latency constraints, NOT just the IGP's shortest cost. MPLS supports SIGNALLED tunnels (LSPs) with explicit-path constraints + bandwidth reservation via RSVP-TE. Which feature?
options: MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE)
MPLS for small networks — wrong scope
A routing protocol — TE is a feature on top of MPLS, not a protocol category
Multicast over MPLS — different feature (mLDP / MVPN)
questions.explanation: MPLS TE uses RSVP-TE to signal explicit LSPs. Routers run OSPF-TE/IS-IS-TE (with TE extensions to share bandwidth info). Offline computation or PCEP/SDN controllers calculate optimal paths. Used for WAN optimization and congestion avoidance.

questions.question: Cisco IOS supports two on-box scripting capabilities: (a) Tcl shell for interactive command sequences, (b) Embedded Event Manager (EEM) for event-triggered automated responses (e.g., 'on interface flap, run a Tcl script + email NOC'). What's correct about IOS scripting?
options: Cisco IOS does not support on-box scripting — false; IOS bundles both a Tcl shell for interactive scripting and EEM (Embedded Event Manager) for event-driven automation
Tcl is a third-party tool that must be installed separately from the IOS image — false; Tcl is bundled inside IOS and activated via the `tclsh` shell command
Cisco IOS includes a Tcl shell for CLI-driven interactive scripting and EEM (Embedded Event Manager) for event-driven automation applets and Tcl scripts
On-box scripting is only available on NX-OS and IOS-XR, not on classic IOS or IOS-XE — false; Tcl shell and EEM are available across IOS, IOS-XE, NX-OS, and IOS-XR
questions.explanation: EEM applets are simple IOS policies: 'event syslog pattern [regex]' triggers 'action cli command [cmd]'. EEM Tcl scripts provide more complex logic. Use cases: auto-recovery, correlation, compliance checks, automated troubleshooting.

questions.question: In DMVPN Phase 2 / 3, a SPOKE wants to talk directly to another SPOKE (not via the hub). It needs to discover the other spoke's PUBLIC (NBMA / underlay) IP from the spoke's overlay tunnel IP. The hub maintains a dynamic mapping table; spokes query it on demand. Which protocol?
options: A VPN encryption protocol — wrong category (IPsec is encryption; NHRP is mapping)
A DHCP alternative — wrong category
A routing protocol — wrong category
NHRP (Next Hop Resolution Protocol)
questions.explanation: In DMVPN, NHRP allows spoke routers to query the hub for the physical (NBMA) address of other spokes, enabling on-demand spoke-to-spoke tunnels without pre-configuring all pairs. Hub maintains NHRP database.

questions.question: Cisco SD-Access uses two complementary segmentation constructs. (A) MACRO segmentation — entire routing domain (VRF-lite-style), separating tenants. (B) MICRO segmentation — 16-bit tag attached to users/devices by ISE; enforcement points compare tags via Cisco TrustSec. Which mapping?
options: Wireless network types — wrong category
VN (Virtual Network) = macro segmentation (per-tenant routing domain)
VLAN alternatives — partial; SD-Access uses VNs/SGTs that subsume some VLAN roles, but the distinction is macro vs micro segmentation
Security zones — too vague
questions.explanation: SD-Access segmentation: VNs (like VRFs) for isolation between major groups (IoT, Guest, Corp). Within a VN, SGTs (1-65535) tag users/endpoints by role. SGACLs (Cisco TrustSec) enforce which SGTs can communicate.

questions.question: A BGP operator tags ROUTES (not peers) with 32-bit values that other ASes can match on to apply policy ('community 65000:100 = customer route', 'community 64512:666 = blackhole'). The values are TRANSITIVE optional attributes carried in BGP UPDATEs. Which BGP attribute?
options: BGP neighbour group / peer-group — groups peers sharing the same outbound policy for operational efficiency; applies policy to peers, not a 32-bit tagging attribute on routes
AS Path prepending — adds the local AS number repeatedly to the AS_PATH attribute to influence best-path selection; a path attribute but not a 32-bit tag carried on routes for transit policy
BGP route reflection — iBGP scaling mechanism using a Route Reflector; changes topology but is not a 32-bit transitive attribute that tags routes for inter-AS routing policy
BGP Communities — well-known or private 32-bit transitive attributes that tag routes; other ASes match on community values to apply routing policy (local-pref, MED, no-export)
questions.explanation: BGP communities: NO_EXPORT (don't advertise beyond AS), NO_ADVERTISE (don't advertise to any peer), LOCAL_AS. Custom communities: 'ip community-list' + route-map to set local-preference, MED, or filter routes based on community tags.

questions.question: A bank's MPLS WAN already provides privacy + segmentation. The bank ADDITIONALLY needs to encrypt traffic between sites without altering the underlying IP headers (so transit MPLS PE/P routers can still forward by label). The Cisco VPN uses GROUP keys — all members share one key + SA. Which technology?
options: GETVPN (Group Encrypted Transport VPN)
Remote-access VPN — different shape (per-user tunnels)
Standard site-to-site IPsec — adds new headers and requires per-pair SAs; doesn't fit
DMVPN variant — different shape (overlay tunnels, not in-place encryption)
questions.explanation: GETVPN uses Tunnel-less encryption (preserves original IP headers) via GET VPN with a Key Server (KS) distributing group keys to Group Members (GMs). Traffic encrypted in place on existing MPLS WAN. No tunneling overhead.

questions.question: An OSPF router has TWO equal-cost paths to the same destination. Cisco IOS installs BOTH next-hops in the FIB and load-balances packets across them per-destination (default) or per-flow (CEF hashing). Which feature is this?
options: A QoS mechanism — different concept
STP variant — wrong layer
A routing protocol — feature within protocols, not a protocol itself
ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path)
questions.explanation: ECMP: if multiple routes to same destination with equal metric exist, traffic distributed across all (per-destination or per-packet). Default ECMP: 4 paths (IOS), up to 16 configurable. EIGRP supports unequal-cost load balancing (variance command).

questions.question: An enterprise has two upstream ISPs. They WANT inbound internet traffic to PREFER ISP-A. They control their OWN AS but not the global internet's. They add their own AS multiple times to the AS_PATH attribute when advertising to ISP-B — making the route via ISP-B look longer. Other ASes prefer ISP-A's shorter path. Which technique?
options: Shorten AS path for faster routing — false; this technique LENGTHENS the path on purpose
Remove AS numbers — false; they're added, not removed
Filter by AS — different concept (AS-path filter ACL)
AS Path prepending
questions.explanation: AS path prepending adds your ASN multiple times to the AS_PATH of routes advertised to specific ISPs. Longer AS path = less preferred. Used for inbound traffic engineering: prefer ISP-A over ISP-B by prepending on ISP-B advertisements.

questions.question: Cisco's Trustworthy Systems initiative for routers/switches includes: (a) a hardware ROOT OF TRUST stored in a TAm (Tamper-resistant Anchor module) chip, (b) Secure Boot validating signature of each boot stage, (c) Image Signing of IOS, (d) Run-time defences against tampering. What is the goal?
options: Hardware Root of Trust + Secure Boot +
A routing protocol — wrong category
A firewall product — wrong category
An authentication system — wrong category
questions.explanation: Cisco Trustworthy Systems: TAm/SUDI chips provide hardware identity. Secure Boot verifies IOS code signatures. ACT2 (Anti-Counterfeiting Technology 2) prevents fake hardware. Network operators can verify device authenticity cryptographically. code signing, SUDI (Secure Unique Device Identity) certificates, and TAm (Trust Anchor Module) ensuring Cisco devices boot trusted code and can be cryptographically identified

questions.question: A modern data centre replaces 3-tier (core / aggregation / access) with a TOPOLOGY where every leaf switch connects to every spine switch directly. Latency is constant (1 hop leaf→spine→leaf), bandwidth scales by adding spines, and every link is utilised via ECMP. What's this called?
options: Leaf-spine fabric
A VLAN architecture — wrong category
Network monitoring system — wrong category
Physical cable-management system — wrong category
questions.explanation: Leaf-Spine fabric: every leaf switch connects to every spine switch (no leaf-to-leaf or spine-to-spine connections). Benefits: any-to-any East-West traffic in 2 hops, ECMP across all spines, add capacity by adding leaf+spine pairs.

questions.question: Polling devices every 5 minutes via SNMP gives lossy, low-resolution data. A modern alternative has devices PUSH structured telemetry to collectors via gRPC / gNMI / NETCONF every 1 s — using YANG models for schema. Which is which?
options: MDT and SNMP are functionally identical — false; MDT pushes YANG-modelled telemetry data over gRPC/gNMI subscriptions; SNMP pulls scalar MIB OIDs on a polling timer
MDT requires special hardware modules not supported on standard Cisco platforms — false; MDT with gRPC/gNMI and YANG models is supported on IOS-XE, IOS-XR, and NX-OS
MDT = push-based streaming telemetry over gRPC/gNMI with YANG models, providing sub-second granularity; SNMP = pull-based polling with MIB OIDs and 5-minute typical intervals
SNMP is the modern standard and MDT is the legacy approach — reversed; MDT with gRPC/gNMI/YANG is the modern streaming telemetry alternative to polling-based SNMP
questions.explanation: MDT streams data in real-time using gRPC/gNMI with YANG models — sub-second updates possible. SNMP GET polls every 5+ minutes. MDT used with InfluxDB/Grafana, Prometheus, or vendor platforms for real-time network observability.

questions.question: A telco service provider uses an orchestration platform that: (a) ABSTRACTS device-vendor differences with YANG models, (b) USES Network Element Drivers (NEDs) to talk to each vendor's southbound API, (c) Provides SERVICE-level templates ('order a customer L3VPN — instantiate VRFs + BGP peers + ACLs + QoS across 6 devices atomically'). Which Cisco product?
options: Cisco NSO (Network Services Orchestrator) — abstracts vendor differences across multi-vendor network devices, provides service model abstraction (YANG/FASTMAP), and supports declarative intent-based orchestration
Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center — a security operations platform for firewall policy management; does not abstract network device vendor APIs or orchestrate services across routers/switches
Cisco Crosswork Network Automation — a telemetry and analytics platform focused on network monitoring and closed-loop automation; distinct from NSO's service orchestration layer
Cisco Catalyst Center (DNA Center) — campus network management and SD-Access controller; automates campus policies but is not a multi-domain service orchestration platform like NSO
questions.explanation: NSO uses YANG models + NEDs (vendor-specific drivers) to provide a vendor-neutral abstraction. Services (VPNs, VLAN configs) modeled once, NSO translates to vendor-specific CLI/NETCONF. Supports rollback, dry-run, compliance.

questions.question: An OSPF Area Border Router (ABR) sits between Area 0 and Area 1. It receives intra-area routes from Area 1 (Type 1/2 LSAs) and must propagate REACHABILITY into Area 0 without flooding the raw LSAs. The ABR generates a different LSA Type that SUMMARIZES the prefixes for the other area's routers. Which LSA Type?
options: Router LSA (Type 1) — describes router-local link states; flooded within an area
Summary LSA (Type 3)
ASBR-Summary LSA (Type 4) — describes ASBR location, not inter-area prefixes
AS-External LSA (Type 5) — describes routes redistributed from other protocols, not inter-area
questions.explanation: Type 3 LSAs are generated by ABRs, summarizing networks from non-backbone areas into Area 0 and vice versa. They don't carry the full topology — just the prefix and cost, keeping LSDB smaller in remote areas.

questions.question: An EIGRP configuration migration moves from CLASSIC mode (`router eigrp 100` + per-AF stanzas) to a NEWER mode that: (a) uses NAMED instances, (b) unifies IPv4 + IPv6 in one config block, (c) supports WIDE METRIC (delay in pico-seconds rather than micro-seconds → larger scale), (d) cleaner show-output. Which mode?
options: Cisco-proprietary-only mode — both are Cisco-proprietary; that's not the distinction
EIGRP named mode
EIGRP debug feature — different surface
New naming convention only — superficial answer; named mode is functional, not cosmetic
questions.explanation: Named EIGRP: 'router eigrp NAME' with address-family sections. Wide metrics use 64-bit composite (supports >100Gbps links properly). Backward compatible. All new EIGRP configurations should use named mode.

questions.question: A BGP-running ROUTER wants to prefer one inbound route over another for LOCAL forwarding decisions only — without affecting other routers in the AS. Cisco provides an attribute that is (a) ROUTER-LOCAL (never advertised), (b) Cisco-proprietary, (c) Higher value preferred. Which attribute?
options: BGP Weight
BGP Weight and Local-Pref identical — false; Local-Pref is advertised to iBGP peers, Weight is router-local
Local-Pref is router-local — false; Local-Pref is AS-wide via iBGP
Weight is advertised to peers — false; it's strictly local
questions.explanation: BGP path selection: Weight > Local Preference > Locally originated > AS Path > Origin > MED > eBGP > IGP metric > oldest > Router ID. Weight: 0-65535, local only. Local Preference: 0-4294967295, AS-wide, higher = preferred. local to the router only (not advertised to peers), influences outbound path selection per-router. Local Preference: advertised within iBGP AS, influences all routers in the AS for outbound path choice

questions.question: A service provider offers customers an Ethernet-like LAN service across multiple geographic sites — ALL customer sites act as if connected to one giant L2 switch. Bridge MAC learning happens across the SP's MPLS / IP transport. Which technology?
options: Site-to-site IPsec — L3 tunnel, not multipoint L2 bridging
VPLS (Virtual Private LAN Service)
Layer-3 VPN — L3 service, not L2 bridging
DMVPN — Cisco hub-and-spoke overlay, not multipoint L2 SP service
questions.explanation: VPLS creates a distributed virtual switch across provider MPLS network. All customer sites appear in same L2 domain. Uses PWs (pseudowires) between PE routers. Replaced increasingly by EVPN which provides the same service more efficiently.

questions.question: A QoS configuration deals with congestion ALMOST FILLING the queue. Tail-drop (drop the next arrival when queue is full) causes TCP global synchronisation. A smarter mechanism drops packets RANDOMLY before the queue fills, with drop probability weighted by their DSCP / IP-Precedence marking. Which mechanism?
options: WRED (Weighted Random Early Detection)
QoS classification — separate task (matching traffic)
QoS marking — separate task (DSCP setting)
QoS policing — token-bucket rate enforcement, drops or re-marks excess; different from RED-style avoidance
questions.explanation: WRED profiles: min-threshold, max-threshold, drop probability. Between min/max: random drops proportional to congestion. Above max: drop all. Different profiles per DSCP class. Prevents tail-drop TCP sync where all TCP flows simultaneously reduce rate.

questions.question: An enterprise compares traditional CLI-and-paste management with Cisco's modern controller-based approach. The controller provides: intent-based design, graphical workflow, ML-based assurance, RESTful APIs, programmable telemetry, multi-vendor management via plug-ins. What is correct?
options: CLI is more reliable — context-dependent; controllers can roll back changes the CLI can't
Identical functionality — false
Catalyst Center has no API — false; APIs are central
Catalyst Center (DNA Center)
questions.explanation: Catalyst Center provides: Design (site hierarchy, templates), Policy (SGT-based via ISE), Provision (zero-touch PnP), Assurance (AI health scores, root cause). REST/RESTCONF APIs. Replaces manual CLI for enterprise scale. policy-driven, REST API, automated provisioning, AI assurance, single pane of glass. CLI: device-by-device, manual, error-prone at scale, no correlation — manages hundreds of devices vs thousands

questions.question: Cisco IOS XE supports running CUSTOM scripts on the device itself via a Linux container called Guestshell. Engineers can run Python 3 scripts that call NETCONF/RESTCONF, react to EEM events, and write to syslog — without any external scripting host. What is this called?
options: IOS XE doesn't support scripting — false
Requires special hardware — false; Guestshell ships with IOS XE
On-box Python 3 in IOS XE Guestshell
Only NX-OS — false; IOS XE supports Guestshell + Python
questions.explanation: IOS XE guestshell: Linux container with Python 3, pip. Can import CLI outputs via subprocess, use NETCONF to the local device, respond to EEM events. Scripts run directly on the device — no controller needed for simple automation.

questions.question: Every OSPF router runs the SHORTEST-PATH-FIRST algorithm over its Link-State Database to compute a tree rooted at ITSELF, finding shortest paths to every destination prefix. The algorithm runs at startup, on every topology change (LSA add/remove), and on a configurable SPF-throttle timer. Which algorithm?
options: Dijkstra's SPF
Only on new routes — false; runs on any topology change
Every 10 seconds — false; only on triggers + throttled re-run
Only at startup — false; runs whenever the LSDB changes
questions.explanation: Full SPF: computationally expensive, triggered by Type 1/2 LSA changes (topology). Partial Route Calculation (PRC): less expensive, triggered by Type 3-7 LSA changes (prefix changes). SPF timers: initial delay + incremental backoff prevent oscillation.

questions.question: In MPLS the egress PE-router would have to do BOTH a label-lookup AND a separate IP lookup if the last label is left on the packet. An optimisation lets the SECOND-TO-LAST router POP the label so the egress PE only does an IP lookup. Which MPLS feature?
options: A BGP optimisation — wrong layer
An MPLS security feature — wrong category
QoS marking — wrong category
PHP (Penultimate Hop Popping)
questions.explanation: PHP: implicit null label (3) signals penultimate router to pop. Egress LSR does only IP lookup, not MPLS+IP. Ultimate Hop Popping (UHP): explicit null label (0) — label kept until egress for QoS or tracking purposes.

questions.question: A source-routing paradigm encodes the path in the packet itself. The INGRESS router pushes a STACK of Segment IDs (SIDs) onto the header; intermediate routers swap/pop SIDs to follow the explicit path. Uses MPLS or IPv6 SRH (Segment Routing Header). No per-flow state in the core. Which paradigm?
options: An IP routing protocol — wrong category
A BGP extension — partial; SR-BGP exists but SR itself is a paradigm
A switching protocol — wrong category
Segment Routing (SR)
questions.explanation: SR-MPLS: SIDs encoded as MPLS labels. SR-v6: SIDs in IPv6 header extension. Topology learned via IGP extensions (OSPF-SR, IS-IS-SR). Benefits: source routing, traffic engineering without per-flow signaling, ECMP, fast reroute.

questions.question: A Cisco chassis with redundant Route Processors (RPs) maintains forwarding during an RP failover. The ACTIVE RP continuously syncs control-plane state (RIB, FIB, adjacencies, protocol state) to the STANDBY RP. On failover, the standby takes over in milliseconds with NO route flap (the FIB stays programmed). What's this feature pair?
options: An HSRP enhancement — wrong product (HSRP is first-hop redundancy)
A spanning-tree feature — wrong layer
A backup routing protocol — wrong category
NSF + SSO
questions.explanation: Without NSF/SSO: RP failure = routing restart = traffic loss during convergence. With SSO: standby RP fully synchronized, sub-second failover. With NSF: keeps forwarding during reconvergence. OSPF/BGP/EIGRP-aware NSF helpers exist.

questions.question: An engineer redistributes EIGRP routes into OSPF. By default OSPF assigns an external metric of 20 to redistributed routes. Without explicitly setting a metric, all redistributed routes get the same default — which makes load balancing and tie-breaking unpredictable. Which best practice handles the metric?
options: Controls hop count — OSPF doesn't use hop count
Route preference — preference is via admin distance, not metric
When redistributing into OSPF, the metric MUST be set
Sets AS path length — that's BGP, not OSPF
questions.explanation: OSPF external types: E2 (default): constant metric end-to-end, cost = external metric only. E1: metric increases by OSPF cost of path to ASBR + external metric. E1 preferred over E2 if both exist for same prefix. you must set a seed metric — default external metric is 20 (E2 type, cost doesn't increase hop-by-hop). E1 type: cost accumulates as packets traverse OSPF topology

questions.question: Cisco SD-WAN's control plane has THREE planes split across three named components: (A) MANAGEMENT (config UI, policy editor, monitoring), (B) CONTROL (computes overlay routes, distributes them to edge routers), (C) ORCHESTRATION (initial onboarding, NAT traversal helper). Which mapping?
options: All three are legacy SD-WAN components replaced by Cisco Catalyst Center — false; vManage, vSmart, and vBond are the current Cisco SD-WAN control plane architecture

vManage, vSmart, and vBond are three names for the same physical controller that handles management, control plane routing, and orchestration simultaneously — false; they are three distinct functional components
vManage = management plane (GUI/API/config), vSmart = control plane (OMP routing policy), vBond = orchestration plane (authentication/NAT traversal for edge-to-controller connectivity)
vManage, vSmart, and vBond are hardware-only appliances; software implementations are not supported in Cisco SD-WAN deployments — false; all three can run as virtual machines
questions.explanation: SD-WAN planes: Management (vManage: telemetry, templates, policies), Control (vSmart: OMP routes, policy enforcement, key distribution), Data (vEdge/cEdge: IPsec tunnels, forwarding), Orchestration (vBond: initial device onboarding, NAT discovery). API, policy config). vSmart: control plane (OMP routing protocol, policy distribution). vBond: orchestration plane (initial authentication, NAT traversal for WAN edges)

questions.question: In LISP, every packet to a new EID would normally trigger a Map-Request to the Map Server. Sub-second performance requires caching the EID-to-RLOC binding LOCALLY at the LISP router so subsequent packets to the same destination skip the lookup. What is this?
options: A BGP route cache — different surface
LISP Map Cache
A routing table entry — different data structure
DNS caching — different surface
questions.explanation: LISP first packet: ITR sends Map-Request to Map-Resolver → Map-Server → responds with RLOC. ITR caches EID→RLOC mapping. Subsequent packets: encapsulate directly using cached RLOC. Map-Cache: show lisp site / show lisp map-cache.

questions.question: Cisco TrustSec assigns each AUTHENTICATED endpoint a 16-bit GROUP TAG by ISE. Switches and routers carry the tag inline with packets (inline tagging or via SXP). Enforcement is at the egress device — comparing src + dst tags against an access matrix. The model decouples policy from IP / VLAN. What is this tag?
options: A routing protocol — wrong category
A VPN technology — wrong category
SGT (Scalable Group Tag)
An encryption standard — wrong category
questions.explanation: TrustSec propagation: Inline tagging (hardware support, L2 tag preserved hop-to-hop), SXP (software protocol mapping SGT to IP for non-TrustSec devices). SGACLs enforced at egress switch or ASA/FTD based on source/destination SGT pair.

questions.question: Service-provider MPLS L3VPN delivers separate routing tables per customer. Each customer's routes are kept distinct via (a) VRFs on PE routers, (b) MP-BGP carrying VPNv4 prefixes (= RD-prefix + RT), (c) MPLS labels in the data plane for tenant-segregated forwarding. Which is correct?
options: Customer-managed firewall segmentation — each customer deploys their own firewall to segment traffic; the SP network carries the traffic transparently without per-customer VRFs
Customer VRFs (Virtual Routing and Forwarding instances) on PE routers plus MP-BGP with the VPNv4 address family to carry customer routes with Route Distinguishers across the SP MPLS core
Customer-managed GRE tunnels — customers build point-to-point GRE tunnels over the SP network for separation; the SP does not maintain per-customer routing tables

A generic MPLS tunneling protocol that labels packets for switching — MPLS provides the forwarding but does not itself create separate customer routing tables; VRFs + MP-BGP provide the L3VPN separation
questions.explanation: MPLS L3VPN: CE connects to PE (eBGP/static/OSPF). PE imports routes into VRF, redistributes into MP-BGP VPNv4. RT import/export controls which VPNs receive which routes. P routers: no customer routes, only label forwarding. Two labels: outer (LSP) + inner (VRF).

questions.question: An automation team contrasts SSH/CLI scripting with NETCONF. NETCONF offers: a CANDIDATE config datastore (changes staged before commit), TRANSACTIONS (commit-all or rollback-all atomically), LOCK on the running datastore (exclusive write), structured XML / JSON output with YANG schemas, and named operations (`get-config`, `edit-config`, `commit`). Which describes NETCONF's advantages?
options: CLI over SSH provides better error handling and structured transaction feedback than NETCONF — false; CLI returns unstructured text; NETCONF returns structured XML with explicit error codes
NETCONF provides atomic transactions (candidate datastore, lock, commit, rollback), structured XML/YANG data, and explicit error codes — purpose-built for programmatic config management
NETCONF is slower than CLI because of XML parsing overhead and the candidate datastore lock mechanism — false; structured parsing eliminates screen-scraping; performance depends on implementation
NETCONF and CLI are functionally equivalent for programmatic configuration — false; NETCONF has a candidate datastore for staged commits, model-driven validation, and lock semantics absent from CLI
questions.explanation: NETCONF operations: get-config, edit-config (merge/replace/create/delete), commit, lock/unlock, validate. Candidate datastore: edit without affecting running config, then commit atomically. On error: automatic rollback. Critical for safe automation.

questions.question: An ABR sits at the boundary between Area 0 and Area 1. It maintains: (a) ONE LSDB per area (one for Area 0, one for Area 1), (b) Translates intra-area routes into Type-3 Summary LSAs for the OTHER area. It does NOT merge the LSDBs. The benefit is constraining LSA flooding scope. Which behaviour describes ABRs?
options: ABR floods all LSA types everywhere — false; flooding is area-scoped
ABR maintains separate LSDB per area, generates Type-3 Summary LSAs to
ABR only in backbone — false; ABR by definition touches Area 0 + another area
ABR merges LSDBs — false; LSDBs stay separate per area
questions.explanation: ABR: interface in Area 0 + at least one other area. Separate LSDB per area. Generates Type 3 LSAs from intra-area prefixes. Can summarize: 'area X range prefix mask' reduces Type 3 LSAs. Prevents discontiguous areas via virtual-link. runs SPF per area, generates Type 3 Summary LSAs to advertise prefixes between areas. Summary routes can be configured to reduce inter-area LSA count

questions.question: An NetFlow capability records IP flows. Standard NetFlow has FIXED key fields (5-tuple). The MODERN evolution lets the operator DEFINE: which keys to use (e.g., source-IP + ToS only), which non-key fields to collect (interfaces, byte counts, TCP flags, AS path), and which exporters / collectors to send to — per cache. Which feature?
options: Flexible NetFlow
An IOS version — wrong category
QoS mechanism — wrong category
Routing protocol — wrong category
questions.explanation: Flexible NetFlow: flow record (define keys + non-key fields), flow exporter (IPFIX/NetFlow v9 to collector), flow monitor (combines record + exporter, applied to interface). Collectors: SolarWinds, PRTG, ntopng, ELK stack.

questions.question: A hub-and-spoke WAN uses EIGRP. Spokes have ONE upstream interface to the hub and no transit role. To prevent the hub from using a spoke as a transit path (spoke-A → hub → spoke-B → hub → spoke-A loop possibility) AND to suppress unnecessary queries to spokes during DUAL convergence, the spokes are configured with a specific EIGRP feature. Which?
options: EIGRP Stub routing
Disable EIGRP on stub interfaces — different goal
Reduce EIGRP table — partial side-effect, not the primary mechanism
Enable EIGRP over WAN — generic, doesn't match the specific feature
questions.explanation: EIGRP stub router (spoke): 'eigrp stub connected summary'. Hub won't send Queries to stub routers (can't be used as transit). Reduces query domain scope dramatically in large hub-and-spoke topologies, preventing SIA (Stuck In Active) scenarios.

questions.question: A Cisco ACI tenant has an EPG (Endpoint Group) defined by VLAN-200. Inside that EPG the SecOps team wants tighter policy: VMs whose name starts with `prod-` get one contract; VMs whose name starts with `dev-` get a different contract — REGARDLESS of port/VLAN. ACI extends EPG membership criteria beyond port/VLAN. What's this called?
options: VLAN-based segmentation — what's being EXTENDED, not the answer
ACI Microsegmentation (uSeg)
Routing segmentation — VRF-level, different scope
A firewall feature — wrong product
questions.explanation: uSeg (microsegmentation) EPGs: endpoints automatically assigned based on attributes learned from VMware vCenter, Kubernetes, or IP/MAC criteria. Same physical network, policy enforced per-VM based on identity, not location.

questions.question: An OSPF design has a non-backbone Area 2 that was provisioned without a direct attachment to Area 0 (Area 1 sits between Area 2 and Area 0). OSPF requires every non-backbone area to TOUCH Area 0. A temporary fix lets Area 2's ABR reach Area 0 through Area 1 logically — without an actual transit circuit. Which OSPF construct?
options: A backup link — wrong concept
A multi-area OSPF feature — too vague
Virtual link
WAN tunnel — wrong layer (the virtual link is OSPF logical)
questions.explanation: Virtual link: configured between two ABRs across a transit area. Makes the non-connected area appear directly connected to Area 0. Not recommended for permanent designs — indicates poor topology. Transit area must not be stub/NSSA.

questions.question: An ops team wants ACTIVE measurement of network performance: send synthetic ICMP / UDP / HTTP / DNS / VoIP probes, record one-way and round-trip latency / jitter / loss, and alert / failover based on thresholds. The probes originate from IOS itself. Which Cisco IOS feature?
options: A routing protocol — wrong category
A QoS tool — wrong category
IP SLA
An SLA document — that's a contract, not a feature
questions.explanation: IP SLA: 'ip sla 1' define operation (icmp-echo, udp-jitter). 'ip sla schedule'. 'show ip sla statistics'. Track SLA with 'track 1 ip sla 1 reachability' → use in routing: 'ip route ... track 1' (floating static based on reachability).

questions.question: A multi-WAN-path enterprise (MPLS + broadband + LTE) wants APPLICATION-aware path choice: VoIP must always take the lowest-jitter path, large file copies the cheapest, web traffic the lowest-latency. The decision is RE-EVALUATED per real-time IP-SLA metric. Which Cisco IWAN feature?
options: Firewall feature — wrong category
Routing protocol — wrong category
QoS mechanism — wrong category
PfRv3 (Performance Routing)
questions.explanation: PfRv3/IWAN: master controller monitors path performance via IP SLA probes, moves traffic between MPLS/broadband based on policy thresholds per application class. Replaced by Cisco SD-WAN (Viptela) which does the same more elegantly.

questions.question: A multi-homed AS advertises the same prefix to two upstream peers via two PE routers. The AS wants peers to PREFER ONE entry point over the other. The BGP attribute that hints inbound preference to neighbours is LOWER-VALUE-PREFERRED and is only compared between routes received from the SAME neighbouring AS. Which attribute?
options: BGP MED (Multi-Exit Discriminator)
Always used across all peers — false; only between routes from the same AS by default
A security metric — false
Controls outbound traffic — false; MED is for INBOUND traffic
questions.explanation: MED (metric): advertised to eBGP peers to suggest preferred ingress point. Lower = preferred. Default: compare MED only from same AS ('bgp always-compare-med' to compare across all ASes, but creates routing instability risk). Set with route-map 'set metric'.

questions.question: EVPN defines several BGP NLRI route TYPES carried in the MP-BGP control plane. (Type 2) Advertises a host's MAC + optional IP — used for L2 VPN MAC learning over the control plane. (Type 5) Advertises an IP prefix for L3 routing across the EVPN fabric. Which mapping is correct?
options: OSPF LSA types — wrong protocol
Firewall rule types — wrong category
Type 2 = MAC/IP Advertisement (L2 MAC learning
BGP version numbers — false; route types are NLRI classes
questions.explanation: EVPN Route Types: 1 (Ethernet Auto-Discovery: multi-homing), 2 (MAC/IP: L2 forwarding), 3 (Inclusive Multicast: BUM traffic), 4 (ES Route: multi-homing redundancy), 5 (IP Prefix: L3 routing). Type 2+5 most common in data center fabrics.

questions.question: An OSPF router is undergoing a software upgrade. Without intervention, every NEIGHBOUR would tear down adjacencies, recompute SPF, and route around it — causing a transient outage. A capability lets the restarting router KEEP its adjacencies + the data-plane forwarding while it rebuilds the OSPF process. Which feature?
options: A debugging feature — wrong category
OSPF Graceful Restart (RFC 3623)
Planned maintenance generally — too vague
A stub area feature — different mechanism
questions.explanation: Graceful restart: restarting router signals helpers via Grace LSA. Helpers maintain adjacency and don't originate topology changes during grace period (default 120s). Allows ISSU (In-Service Software Upgrade) without dropping OSPF routes.

questions.question: A service provider replaces hardware appliances (firewall, load balancer, WAN optimiser, IDS) with SOFTWARE versions running on COMMODITY x86 servers — chained together by an orchestrator. CapEx drops, deployment speed rises, and the network becomes programmable. What's this called?
options: Software-defined WAN — different concept (SDN of the WAN itself)
Virtualized routers only — too narrow; NFV covers many appliance types
Network Function Virtualisation (NFV)
A type of hypervisor — false; NFV runs ON a hypervisor
questions.explanation: NFV decouples network functions from hardware: virtual firewall (ASAv, Palo Alto VM), virtual router (CSR1000V, vMX), virtual load balancer (F5 BIG-IP VE). Managed via NFVO (NFV Orchestrator) like Cisco NSO or OpenStack Tacker.

questions.question: A branch router has a primary WAN to the HQ via MPLS and a backup via internet. PBR routes specific source-IPs via the MPLS path. The team adds IP-SLA probes through the MPLS path with object-tracking: if probes fail, the PBR rule is dynamically disabled and traffic falls back to the default route via internet. Which combination is this?
options: PBR + IP-SLA object-tracking
A routing protocol — too generic
BGP multihoming — different mechanism
Firewall failover — wrong product
questions.explanation: Example: PBR route-map matches HTTP traffic, sets next-hop to MPLS if SLA probe up, internet if down. 'set ip next-hop verify-availability [IP] [seq] track [obj]'. Multiple next-hops tried in order until verified reachable.

questions.question: Two MPLS LSRs lose the direct link between them. Without intervention their LDP session — established over that link — would tear down, label bindings lost. A feature establishes a TARGETED LDP session over ALTERNATE paths so labels survive direct-link failure. Which feature?
options: Security protocol — wrong category
QoS feature — wrong category
LDP Session Protection
LDP encryption — different concern (security, not survivability)
questions.explanation: LDP session protection: configure targeted LDP sessions between routers in addition to link-local LDP. If direct link fails, targeted session maintains LDP bindings via alternate path. Dramatically reduces convergence time when link restores.

questions.question: A BGP router is undergoing a planned restart. Normally its eBGP neighbours would tear down adjacency and withdraw the routes. A feature lets the restarting router signal 'restart in progress' in the BGP OPEN message; helpful neighbours retain its routes (marked stale) and the data plane keeps forwarding while the restart completes. Which feature?
options: Backup BGP — not a real concept
An MPLS feature — wrong layer
BGP Graceful Restart (RFC 4724)
BGP security — wrong category
questions.explanation: BGP GR: restart timer (default 120s). Restarting router maintains forwarding. Helper peers retain stale routes during graceful restart period. After restart, routes re-advertised and stale routes removed. Critical for hitless ISSU on BGP routers.

questions.question: Cisco's HIERARCHICAL campus reference design separates roles. The CORE provides high-speed L3 backbone between buildings. The DISTRIBUTION layer aggregates access switches and applies L3 policy. The ACCESS layer attaches end-hosts. In a SMALLER campus a 2-tier 'COLLAPSED CORE' merges core + distribution. Which mapping is correct?
options: 3-tier always best — context-dependent
Identical — false
2-tier is only small offices — false; small/mid campuses use it routinely
3-tier = Core + Distribution + Access (large
questions.explanation: 3-tier: Core (campus backbone, high-speed, no policy), Distribution (routing, ACL, STP, redundancy per building), Access (PoE, VLANs, 802.1X). 2-tier: eliminate separate core for smaller designs. Modern: spine-leaf replacing 3-tier in many designs.

questions.question: Cisco IOS Embedded Event Manager (EEM) exposes two scripting flavours. (A) APPLETS: inline IOS-config policies with event + ordered action lines — limited logic, no full programming primitives. (B) TCL SCRIPTS: a full programming language with loops + conditionals + sockets — written as .tcl files. Which mapping?
options: EEM Applets support all IOS CLI constructs and Tcl language features — false; Applets are limited to event-action config blocks without loops, variables, or inline logic
EEM Applets and EEM Tcl scripts are identical in capability — false; Applets are inline IOS-config event-action policies; Tcl scripts are full programs with conditionals, loops, and API access
EEM Tcl scripts are deprecated in modern IOS-XE and replaced by Python on-box scripting — false; Tcl scripts are still supported and used for complex logic requiring inline event handling
EEM Applet = simple inline IOS-config policy (event trigger + action list); EEM Tcl script = full Tcl program registered as an event handler with access to loops, variables, and IOS APIs
questions.explanation: EEM applet: 'event manager applet NAME / event syslog pattern / action 1.0 cli command'. Good for simple triggered responses. EEM TCL: register_event, event_reqinfo, full TCL logic. TCL scripts stored in flash or TFTP server. Use applet for simple, TCL for complex automation.

questions.question: HSRP elects an active router based on priority. Without one option, a returning router with a HIGHER priority will NOT take back the active role — the current active keeps it. The option lets a higher-priority router take over the active role when it comes online. Which option, and what risk?
options: Preemption
Preemption causes loops — false; HSRP preempt isn't loop-related
HSRP preempts by default — false; preempt is OFF by default
Preemption is automatic — false; must be explicitly enabled
questions.explanation: HSRP preempt: 'standby 1 preempt delay minimum 60' — delay prevents preemption during routing convergence after reboot. Without preempt: current Active stays until it fails. Best practice: enable preempt + delay on primary router to ensure deterministic active placement.

questions.question: Cisco IOS-XE exposes its config schema in TWO YANG model flavours: (A) Cisco-IOS-XE-native — vendor-specific, mirrors CLI structure (`/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/interface`). (B) OpenConfig — vendor-neutral models from the OpenConfig consortium. NETCONF / RESTCONF clients pick the model on a per-operation basis. Which describes IOS-XE's interface YANG models?
options: Cisco-IOS-XE-native YANG models map the full IOS-XE feature set in a Cisco-proprietary hierarchy; OpenConfig YANG models use vendor-neutral, community-driven schemas for cross-vendor portability
YANG model flavours are a routing protocol extension — false; YANG is a data modelling language defining configuration and state schemas for NETCONF/RESTCONF; unrelated to routing protocol operation
YANG model flavours are a hardware component standard defining physical port schemas — false; YANG models define software config and state schemas, not hardware specs
YANG model flavours are Cisco IOS CLI command variants — false; YANG models are structured data schemas accessed via NETCONF/RESTCONF, not IOS CLI command syntax
questions.explanation: YANG tree for interface: name, type, enabled, ipv4/ipv6 addresses, MTU, description. Accessed via NETCONF get-config/edit-config or RESTCONF GET/PUT/PATCH. 'show yang modules' lists all supported YANG models on device.

questions.question: Cisco SD-Access supports two complementary segmentation models. MACRO uses Virtual Networks (VNs/VRFs) to provide COMPLETE ROUTING ISOLATION between large groups (corporate / IoT / guest). MICRO uses Scalable Group Tags (SGTs) inside a VN to control inter-group access without per-VLAN ACLs. Which mapping?
options: Macro segmentation uses VN/VRF routing tables to provide full Layer-3 isolation between large tenant groups; micro segmentation uses SGTs to enforce per-flow policy within a VN at the fabric edge
Only macro segmentation using VNs is supported in SD-Access — false; SD-Access supports both VN-based macro segmentation for routing isolation and SGT-based micro segmentation within a VN
Micro segmentation requires separate physical hardware to enforce SGT policy independently of the macro segmentation VN routing isolation — false; both run on the same SD-Access fabric nodes
Macro and micro segmentation in SD-Access are different names for the same Virtual Network construct — false; macro uses VRF/VN routing separation while micro uses SGTs for granular per-flow policy
questions.explanation: SD-Access layers: VN (VRF-based, L3 isolation, separate routing table per VN) = macro. SGT (16-bit tag assigned by ISE) = micro. SGACLs: 'permit/deny' between source SGT and destination SGT. Both can coexist — VN isolation + fine-grained role policy within VN.

questions.question: A WAN team needs an encrypted tunnel that ALSO carries non-IP protocols (multicast, OSPF Hellos, IPX, NHRP) over the public internet. Standard IPsec TUNNEL mode encrypts unicast IP only and doesn't expose a routable tunnel interface. The solution: wrap traffic in GRE first (provides a tunnel interface + multicast / any-protocol support) and protect GRE with IPsec. Which?
options: GRE over IPsec
GRE over IPsec and IPsec tunnel-mode identical — false
GRE provides encryption — false; GRE is unencrypted
IPsec supports multicast natively — false; vanilla IPsec doesn't carry multicast
questions.explanation: IPSec transport mode: encrypts payload, original IP header preserved. IPSec tunnel mode: encrypts entire IP packet, new IP header added. GRE+IPSec: GRE creates tunnel interface for routing/multicast, IPSec encrypts GRE packets. Most enterprise VPNs use GRE+IPSec.

questions.question: OSPF runs SPF after every LSDB change. Without dampening, a flapping interface would trigger SPF every few ms — overwhelming the CPU. The router uses configurable timers: INITIAL delay before SPF runs, HOLD-time between subsequent runs (exponential backoff), MAX hold-time ceiling. The purpose: trade-off latency to converge versus CPU stability. What are these timers?
options: Fixed 5-second timers — false; configurable with exponential backoff
Only relevant in large networks — false; all OSPF networks use them
Static 10-second — false; documented as `timers throttle spf <start> <hold> <max>`
OSPF SPF timers (initial / hold / max)
questions.explanation: 'timers throttle spf [initial] [min-between] [max-wait]' in ms. Default: 50ms/200ms/5000ms. During flapping: first SPF fast (50ms), subsequent SPFs progressively slower up to 5s — prevents CPU exhaustion during network instability. LSA throttle timers similarly.

questions.question: A Link Aggregation Group bundles 4 member links into one logical interface. Standard BFD treats the LAG as one session — it cannot tell WHICH member dropped if one fails. A variant runs INDEPENDENT BFD sessions on EACH member link so per-member failure is detected sub-second. Which feature?
options: Monitors LAG aggregate only — that's standard BFD, not Micro-BFD
Only for OSPF — false; Micro-BFD is LAG-specific, layer-2
Standalone protocol — false; an extension of BFD for LAG
Micro-BFD for LAG
questions.explanation: Micro-BFD: per-member-link BFD sessions aggregate into LAG BFD session. If any member BFD session fails, that link removed from LAG immediately. Standard LACP slow timers (30s/90s) = too slow for <1s failure detection. Micro-BFD: millisecond detection.

questions.question: Cisco has shipped two generations of network controllers. (A) APIC-EM (legacy) — initial controller focused on path-trace, IWAN, Plug-and-Play; deprecated 2018. (B) Catalyst Center (originally DNA Center) — modern intent-based platform with assurance / policy / automation. Which mapping?
options: Identical products — false
Different device types — partially true but the BEST answer is the generation/feature distinction
APIC-EM = legacy controller (path-trace, IWAN, PnP,
APIC-EM newer — reversed
questions.explanation: APIC-EM (Application Policy Infrastructure Controller — Enterprise Module): REST-based path analysis, device discovery. DNA Center/Catalyst Center: full SD-Access controller, AI-powered assurance, automated provisioning, PnP, comprehensive APIs. Major architectural upgrade. ACL analysis, EasyQoS). DNA Center: next-generation platform replacing APIC-EM with SD-Access, AI assurance, intent-based networking, full lifecycle management. APIC-EM EOL 2019

questions.question: Two Nexus switches present themselves to a downstream device as a SINGLE logical switch. The downstream device sees ONE port-channel terminating on what looks like one switch (even though the member links land on DIFFERENT physical switches). Active-active across both Nexus boxes, no STP blocking. Which feature?
options: Regular LAG — single switch only, not the dual-switch logical aggregation described
vPC (virtual Port Channel)
Routing protocol — wrong layer
VLAN feature — wrong layer
questions.explanation: vPC: peer keepalive link (management network, detects peer failure), peer link (sync MAC/ARP tables, carry orphan traffic). Downstream device sees one logical switch. Both uplinks active (unlike traditional STP blocking). Critical for ToR switch design.

questions.question: An ALTERNATIVE to BGP Route Reflectors for solving the iBGP full-mesh requirement: split a large AS into smaller sub-ASes (confederation member-ASes). Inside the confederation, member ASes peer with each other via 'intra-confed eBGP'. Externally the whole confederation appears as ONE AS via a configured confederation identifier. Which feature?
options: BGP security feature — wrong category
Route filtering — different concern
BGP Confederation
Path selection — different concept
questions.explanation: Confederation: AS 65000 split into sub-ASes 65001, 65002. Internal sub-ASes use eBGP between them (path selection with eBGP rules) but AS_PATH shows only outer AS 65000 to external peers. More complex than route reflectors but preserves eBGP semantics.

questions.question: An ISP wants to PREVENT BGP route hijacks (an unrelated AS advertising prefixes it doesn't own). A PKI-based system has prefix-holders CRYPTOGRAPHICALLY sign Route Origin Authorisations (ROAs) declaring 'AS-X is authorised to originate prefix P/24'. Routers validate received BGP updates against the RPKI repository and drop invalid origins. Which system?
options: A firewall certificate system — wrong category
RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure)
A DNS security extension (DNSSEC) — wrong protocol
A routing protocol — RPKI is a security framework over BGP, not a routing protocol itself
questions.explanation: RPKI: prefix owner creates ROA (prefix, origin AS, max prefix length) signed by RIR (ARIN, RIPE). BGP routers validate announcements against RPKI validator — Invalid routes rejected/de-preferred. Critical defense against BGP hijacking (like AS 7007, Pakistan Telecom incidents).

questions.question: Two VXLAN data planes: (A) FLOOD-AND-LEARN — each VTEP discovers MACs by flooding BUM traffic across the underlay multicast; no control plane awareness. (B) MP-BGP EVPN — VTEPs advertise MAC + IP bindings in BGP control plane; no flooding required to learn MACs. Which describes the difference?
options: Flood-and-learn VXLAN is more secure than EVPN because BUM traffic is contained within the underlay — false; flooding BUM traffic across the underlay creates unnecessary load and exposure
Flood-and-learn = BUM traffic (Broadcast, Unknown-unicast, Multicast) flooded across the underlay to discover MACs; EVPN control plane = BGP MAC/IP advertisements eliminate BUM flooding
EVPN-based VXLAN is slower than flood-and-learn because BGP MAC/IP advertisements add latency to the BUM-flooding process — false; EVPN eliminates BUM flooding entirely using BGP updates
Flood-and-learn and EVPN VXLAN are identical in their MAC-learning mechanism — false; flood-and-learn uses data-plane BUM flooding while EVPN uses BGP control-plane MAC/IP advertisements
questions.explanation: Flood-and-learn VXLAN: first packet flooded via multicast or head-end replication. EVPN control plane: VTEPs advertise learned MAC/IP via BGP Type 2 routes before traffic arrives — known unicast forwarding, no flooding for unicast. Critical for scale. Unknown, Multicast) traffic flooded to all VTEPs for MAC learning — scales poorly. BGP EVPN: MAC/IP learned via BGP Type 2 routes, no flooding needed for unicast — scales to thousands of VTEPs

questions.question: Two OSPF routers reach 2-Way state. They now must synchronise their LSDBs before reaching FULL adjacency. The process: (a) ExStart — elect Master (higher Router-ID) / Slave; (b) Exchange — trade Database Description packets summarising the LSDB; (c) Loading — request specific LSAs that are missing; (d) Full. Which describes this?
options: OSPF database exchange
DR/BDR only — false; happens between every adjacency pair
Once an hour — false; happens at adjacency formation + on LSDB drift
Continuously — false; only during state transition
questions.explanation: OSPF neighbor states: Down→Attempt→Init→2-Way→ExStart→Exchange→Loading→Full. ExStart: bidirectional communication confirmed, elect Master (sends DBDs first). Exchange: compare LSDBs via DBDs. Loading: request missing LSAs. Full: synced LSDBs, adjacency complete.

questions.question: An MPLS-TE LSP is signalled with two specific constructs. (A) EXPLICIT PATH — operator names the LSP's hops (strict or loose). (B) CSPF (Constrained SPF) — modified Dijkstra that filters out links not meeting bandwidth / affinity constraints, then picks shortest among the remaining. Which describes both?
options: Explicit path = operator-defined node
A general routing-protocol path — too vague
A BGP attribute — wrong protocol
A static route — wrong category
questions.explanation: MPLS-TE: IGP-TE extensions (OSPF-TE/IS-IS-TE) flood bandwidth availability. CSPF calculates path satisfying constraint (e.g., reserve 100Mbps). RSVP-TE signals LSP along calculated path, reserving bandwidth at each hop. Auto-bandwidth adjusts reservations dynamically.

questions.question: A data centre wants WIRE-SPEED HOP-BY-HOP encryption + authentication on every Ethernet link between switches. The encryption is at Layer 2 (after the Ethernet header, before the EtherType payload) so each switch decrypts + re-encrypts at each hop. IEEE 802.1AE defines it. Which standard?
options: L3 encryption — wrong layer (IPsec is L3)
MAC address security feature — different feature (port-security)
MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE)
Wireless-only — false; MACsec is wired Ethernet
questions.explanation: MACsec: encrypts each Ethernet frame between adjacent devices. Use cases: campus distribution-to-core, switch-to-server links. MKA (MACsec Key Agreement) handles key exchange via 802.1X. Different from IPSec (L3) or TLS (L7) — provides L2 encryption.

questions.question: Cisco SD-Access extends to wireless. WLCs run in SD-Access mode, APs operate as 'fabric APs' (FAPs) sending CAPWAP control to the WLC but DATA-PLANE tunnelling directly to the edge node via VXLAN. Wireless clients get an SGT assigned by ISE on auth. Same policy / segmentation applies to wired + wireless. Which describes SD-Access wireless?
options: Only on new APs — partially; SD-Access does need supported APs but the BEST answer is the architectural one
Legacy WLC-only — false; SD-Access requires SD-Access-capable WLC
Separate wireless product — false; SD-Access integrates wireless natively
SD-Access extends fabric to wireless
questions.explanation: SD-Access wireless: Fabric-enabled WLC, fabric-mode APs (AP acts as VXLAN VTEP or tunnels to fabric edge). Client: connects to SSID → WLC assigns VLAN/VN/SGT via ISE → traffic enters fabric → same policy as wired. Seamless roaming within fabric.

questions.question: Cisco NSO 'services' are abstract — operators define a YANG SERVICE MODEL with input parameters (customer name, VPN ID, CE-PE links). NSO MAPS the service model to per-device DEVICE-CONFIG using templates or Python/Java code. Creating / modifying / deleting a service is ATOMIC across all impacted devices. Which describes NSO services?
options: A monitoring service — different surface
A config-backup tool — utility, different
A cloud service — context-dependent
NSO services
questions.explanation: NSO service lifecycle: service create (calculate device config from service parameters), re-deploy (reconcile after out-of-band changes), delete (remove all device config created by service). Service intent tracked — NSO knows what config it owns.

questions.question: An ISP's BGP table has a constantly-flapping customer prefix (link bouncing every few seconds). Without intervention every withdrawal+re-announcement propagates through the global internet routing table. A feature assigns a 'penalty score' on each flap, suppresses the route once a threshold is hit, decays the penalty over time, and re-announces once stable. Which feature?
options: Reduces BGP table size — different goal
Speeds convergence — opposite; route dampening DELAYS announcement
BGP Route Dampening
Filters by community — different feature
