questions.explanation: BGP dampening: half-life (how fast penalty decays), reuse threshold (when to re-advertise suppressed route), suppress limit (when to suppress), max-suppress-time. Now discouraged for iBGP and most eBGP (RFC 7196) — causes excessive suppression of valid routes.

questions.question: An EIGRP router has TWO paths to the same prefix with DIFFERENT metrics. Standard ECMP only load-balances EQUAL-cost paths. EIGRP supports a multiplier called VARIANCE that lets it install paths whose metric is up to `variance × Feasible Distance` of the best, then load-balance them PROPORTIONALLY (more traffic to faster path). Which feature?
options: Sends all traffic on best path — that's the default (no variance)
Splits 50/50 — incorrect; ratio is proportional to the metric ratio
Equal-cost only — that's standard ECMP, not what's described
EIGRP Unequal-Cost Load Balancing
questions.explanation: EIGRP variance: 'variance 2' means install routes with metric up to 2x Successor metric (must meet Feasibility Condition). Traffic proportional: route with metric 1000 gets 2x traffic of route with metric 2000. Unique EIGRP feature — OSPF only supports ECMP.

questions.question: An OSPF sub-second convergence stack combines several mechanisms: (a) BFD detects link down in milliseconds (faster than OSPF Hello); (b) OSPF SPF throttle has short initial delay + exponential backoff; (c) LFA / fast-reroute pre-computes backup next-hop. Which describes OSPF Fast Convergence?
options: BFD + interface-down event triggers
BFD incompatible with OSPF — false
Always 30s — false
Only hello timers — false; full stack matters
questions.explanation: Convergence chain: failure detection (BFD 50ms vs OSPF dead timer 40s) → LSA flood → SPF calc (throttled: 50ms initial) → RIB update → CEF update. With BFD: sub-second. Without: 40s dead timer + SPF + FIB update = 40+ seconds.

questions.question: Cisco offers three multi-chassis switching constructs. (A) Stackwise — two or more access switches stack via physical cables, behave as one virtual switch (Cat 3750/3850/9300). (B) VSS — TWO Cat 6500/4500 chassis act as one logical switch (legacy DC core). (C) vPC — two Nexus switches present a port-channel jointly to a downstream device, but each has its OWN control plane. Which mapping?
options: Identical — false
VSS needs special modules — partially true (VS-S720-10G) but not the distinction asked
Stackwise = physical-cable single-virtual-switch
Only Nexus stacks — false
questions.explanation: Stackwise: physical ring cable, 80Gbps backplane, 9 switches max, single management IP. VSS: active/standby supervisor, full mesh between chassis, geographic separation possible. vPC: most complex, fully independent management, data center focused.

questions.question: A multicast deployment wants Rendezvous Point HA without complex RP-failover protocols. Multiple physical RPs are configured with the SAME anycast IP advertised from each location. Sources / receivers find the topologically CLOSEST RP via unicast routing. MSDP redistributes source-active info between RPs. Which feature?
options: A multicast load balancer — too vague
PIM Anycast RP
Unicast routing feature — that's the mechanism, not the multicast feature name
A PIM version — anycast RP is a configuration, not a protocol version
questions.explanation: Anycast RP: multiple PEs advertise same RP address. Sources/receivers join nearest RP. RPs share source state via MSDP (SA messages) or native Anycast RP (PIM Register). Provides RP redundancy and load distribution without VRRP.

questions.question: A border OSPF router has a default route (0.0.0.0/0) via its ISP installed in the RIB. It needs to ADVERTISE that default into OSPF to all internal routers. Two flavours: with `default-information originate` only if a default already exists in the routing table; with the `always` keyword regardless. Which command?
options: `metric default` — sets metric, doesn't originate
`default-information originate [always]`
Disables OSPF default — opposite
Creates a default in OSPF from scratch — partial truth; the command originates a default into OSPF
questions.explanation: 'default-information originate': router must have 0.0.0.0/0 in routing table (from static or ISP). 'always': originates regardless. 'metric': sets external metric. 'metric-type 1 or 2': E1 accumulates cost, E2 does not. Common at Internet edge.

questions.question: CDP and LLDP advertise device platform / OS version / IP / port / capabilities to LAN neighbours. An attacker on an unauthorised port can read these advertisements to plan their attack. The MITIGATION is to disable CDP/LLDP on UNTRUSTED (access) ports while keeping them on inter-switch trunks for management visibility. Which describes the risk and mitigation?
options: Disable on all interfaces always — over-broad; needed on inter-switch links for ops
CDP/LLDP advertise platform / IOS version / IP / port
No risk — false
Only CDP has the risk — false; LLDP advertises the same
questions.explanation: CDP leak: attacker learns switch model (exploitable vulnerabilities), IOS version, management IP. LLDP has same risk. Best practice: 'no cdp enable' + 'no lldp transmit' + 'no lldp receive' on DMZ/external/user-facing ports. Keep enabled on trunk/uplink ports for topology management. IOS version, IP addresses, interface info — valuable for attackers doing network reconnaissance. Mitigation: disable on external-facing interfaces ('no cdp enable' per interface), enable only on trusted internal ports

questions.question: An OSPF backbone has hundreds of transit links and loopbacks used only for routing. Each appears in every router's LSDB and routing table as an inter-area prefix — bloating LSDB and FIB. A feature lets the router declare specific interfaces as 'do not advertise the prefix' while keeping the adjacency. Which feature?
options: Summarises routes — that's `area … range`, different feature
Disables OSPF on selected interfaces — would lose adjacency
Hides from monitoring — wrong concept
OSPF prefix suppression
questions.explanation: 'ip ospf prefix-suppression' per-interface or globally. Transit p2p links: no need to advertise /30 or /31 prefix since hosts never need to reach those IPs directly. Reduces LSDB, hides infrastructure topology. Don't suppress loopbacks used for management.

questions.question: An AS has TWO BGP route reflectors for redundancy. Routes reflected by RR-A could loop back to RR-A via RR-B and clients. A 4-byte attribute is added by RRs to detect that a route has already passed through their cluster — and rejected. What's that attribute?
options: BGP routing domain ID — vague
BGP AS number — wrong attribute
BGP Cluster ID + Cluster List
BGP policy attribute — too vague
questions.explanation: RR cluster: one or more RRs serving a set of clients. Cluster-ID in CLUSTER_LIST prevents loops between RRs. Best practice: multiple RRs per cluster for redundancy. Clients peer with all RRs in cluster. RRs in different clusters exchange routes directly. clients only reflect to clients in same cluster. Multiple RRs in same cluster share same cluster-id to prevent routing loops. Loop prevention: CLUSTER_LIST attribute checked for own cluster-id

questions.question: A network operator upgrades the IOS on a core router WITHOUT a maintenance window. Traffic must continue forwarding; routing protocol adjacencies must NOT flap. The operation requires: (a) redundant supervisors with NSF / SSO, (b) compatible OS versions side-by-side (forward+backward compat), (c) ISSU-aware feature image. What's this called?
options: In-Service Software Upgrade (ISSU)
Regular software update — would require maintenance window
Requires maintenance window — false; ISSU avoids it
ASR-only — false; available on many Cisco platforms
questions.explanation: ISSU process: standby RP upgraded first, switchover (SSO), active RP upgraded, switchover back. Throughout: NSF maintains forwarding, SSO maintains protocol states. Requires: SSO configured, NSF for OSPF/BGP/EIGRP, ISSU-capable hardware, compatible versions.

questions.question: A retail enterprise uses its Wi-Fi infrastructure for INDOOR LOCATION SERVICES — tracking connected devices, generating heatmaps, exposing APIs for marketing apps (welcome messages, dwell-time analytics). The service is cloud-based and integrates with WLCs and APs. What's this service?
options: A security service — different surface
A routing platform — wrong category
Cloud DNS — wrong service
Cisco DNA Spaces (now Spaces)
questions.explanation: DNA Spaces: uses Cisco AP RSSI data for location. REST APIs for app integration. Use cases: retail analytics (dwell time, path analysis), hospital asset tracking, workplace occupancy. Requires Catalyst Center + CMX license or DNA Spaces subscription.

questions.question: Cisco SD-Access deployments separate the fabric into discrete role types running on the underlay. Which TWO statements about SD-Access fabric roles are correct?
options: The Control Plane Node runs the LISP map server / resolver, tracking endpoint-to-RLOC mappings inside the fabric
Border Nodes connect the SD-Access fabric to networks outside the fabric (internet, data centre, legacy domains), performing LISP-to-IP encapsulation/decapsulation
Edge Nodes are the WAN-facing routers that handle MPLS labels for inter-site SD-WAN traffic — false: that role belongs to SD-WAN, not SD-Access
Fabric APs serve as the LISP control plane for wired endpoints — false: APs handle wireless clients; the control-plane role is held by a dedicated node
questions.explanation: In SD-Access, border nodes egress to non-fabric networks; control-plane nodes run LISP and store EID-to-RLOC mappings. Edge nodes do route (they're the L3 anycast gateway for endpoints). The underlay uses VXLAN encapsulation, not MPLS.
